summary: Grand Canyon fire tower built 1928 at Bright Angel Point; moved in 1933 to the north entrance as North Rim Lookout, which still stands. The original site is gone.

facts.status_note: Original Bright Angel Point site is gone; the tower was moved in 1933 and stands at the park's north entrance as North Rim Lookout

staffing.status: no longer used for fire detection

access.note: Intermountain Histories says the North Rim Lookout Tower is available to hikers; no source says whether the cab is open to visitors

events.note: Steel tower about 75 feet tall built at Bright Angel Point, replacing a Forest Service wooden platform
Civilian Conservation Corps moved the tower to the park's north entrance; it became known as North Rim Lookout (about fourteen miles away, per Intermountain Histories)

corrections.why: The original Bright Angel Point site is gone, but the tower was moved in 1933 and still stands at the north entrance as North Rim Lookout (NHLR US 804, AZ 69). 'Gone' describes only the original site.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: National Historic Lookout Register and the Grand Canyon history site say Aermotor; Intermountain Histories says Aeromotor Company. The sources agree on the 1928 steel tower; only the spelling differs.

The Grand Canyon history page says Abbey spent several summers manning the tower and, in another passage, worked four seasons there. Intermountain Histories dates four seasons to the late 1960s and early 1970s. The sources do not reconcile the two counts, and the story reports both.

notes_for_editor: The brief's 'gone' status describes only the original Bright Angel Point site; the tower itself was moved in 1933 and still stands as North Rim Lookout (NHLR US 804, AZ 69). Check whether a separate record already exists for North Rim Lookout before adding a new one. The Stephen Pyne point is second-hand through Intermountain Histories; Pyne's book was not read. 'Available to hikers' comes from one source only. The NPS North Rim status page was read, but its closure lists were ambiguous, so no current closure claim is made. The 1933 move is dated by NHLR and Grand Canyon history; the Abbey years are not dated precisely enough to add as events.
